profile.summary: Lamentations is a collection of five highly elaborate and intensely emotional poems that mourn the destruction of Jerusalem. The book is born from the shock of a ruined nation: after a long siege, Babylon broke the defenses of the city, deported part of Judah and devastated Jerusalem, including the Temple. Although suffering is extreme, the book is not limited to lament; it also interprets the catastrophe as God's just judgment on the sin of his people and keeps open the possibility of mercy, repentance, and restoration. Tradition has associated the book to Jeremiah, but authorship is not explicitly informed in the text itself and the question is debated; the date is put in the immediate context of the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, although the exact composition remains uncertain.
profile.setting: The setting is Jerusalem shortly after a prolonged siege and its fall to Babylon. The city was destroyed, the Temple of God was devastated, many inhabitants of Judah were brought into exile and few survivors remained on earth, among them Jeremiah, according to tradition. The environment is of material ruin, public humiliation, famine, mourning and despair, but also of theological reflection on the faithfulness of God, his righteousness and his mercy.

structure.label: Jerusalem in ruins
structure.description: The city is presented as a rather honored figure and now humiliated, wounded and ashamed; it recognizes its guilt and pleads relief from the Lord.

structure.label: The Shame of Devastation
structure.description: The lament describes the collective misery in Jerusalem: hungry children, mothers in mourning, deceiving prophets and scoffing enemies; tragedy is seen as a result of the withdrawal of divine mercy and promised judgment.

structure.label: The testimony of suffering and the rebirth of hope
structure.description: The author speaks as a witness of divine wrath, crushed by pain and shame, but then recognizes that God's wrath does not last forever and that his faithfulness, love and goodness sustain hope, even with continuous tears.

structure.label: Before and after the collapse
structure.description: The poem counterposes the old glory of the city to the miserable state after the breach of the walls, emphasizing that judgment came in response to the grave sins of the people and that there was no escape from divine discipline.

structure.label: Last supplication for attention and salvation
structure.description: The book ends with a prayer that asks God to carefully consider the situation of the people and with an appeal for salvation, if it is still granted.

themes: I love, shame and collective ruin
Hope in the midst of pain
readingKeys: Notice the contrast between the glorious past of Jerusalem and its present condition of humiliation and loss.
Note how suffering is presented not only as political tragedy, but as a moral and spiritual consequence of the sin of the people.
Follow the passage of pain to hope in chapter 3, where the text states that the wrath of God is real, but it is not eternal.
profile.cautions: The book does not identify its author, although Jeremiah is traditionally linked to it; this attribution is plausible, but not certain, and some scholars defend another later origin. The date is also approximate, located in the period of the fall of Jerusalem, without the exact moment of the essay being proven. The genre is poetic and highly structured: chapters 1 to 4 follow an alphabetic arrangement of Hebrew, a resource that is lost in translation, and this should guide reading without forcing a narrative linearity that the book does not intend to have.

dossier.narratedEra: The poems are set in the catastrophe of the fall of Jerusalem and Judah before Babylon, with the city surrounded, hungry, invaded, and then devastated. The notes place this crisis in the immediately preceding period and after the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC, with the exile and destruction of the temple as the main backdrop.
dossier.compositionEra: The composition is presented in the notes as linked to this same period of calamity, with strong traditional association with Jeremiah, which would have written the laments during or shortly after the destruction. At the same time, Tyndale's introduction acknowledges that the book does not identify the author and mentions that some scholars attribute it to a later author; Matthew Henry also records traditional alternative proposals, but considers them unfounded or unlikely. Thus, the setting and date of writing are close, but the authorship remains debated in the notes.

politics.title: Babylonian rule over Jerusalem
politics.detail: The city was taken after a long siege by the Babylonian army; Babylon overthrew the defenses, took control and destroyed Jerusalem and the temple.
politics.readingImpact: Reading becomes that of a city-state devastated by an imperial power, not just of abstract suffering. This intensifies the weight of the lamentations as a reaction to a political, military and cultual defeat.

politics.title: Alliances frustrated with Egypt
politics.detail: Lamentations 1:2 is explained as a reference to the "lovers" and to the political friends of Judah, especially Egypt, who could not help Jerusalem against Babylon.
politics.readingImpact: The political picture shows that external support has failed. The pain of the text includes the frustration of trusting human alliances incapable of saving the city.

politics.title: Rebellion against the true God and against the invaders permitted by God
politics.detail: The notes link the ruin of Judah to his rebel against God and resist the invaders he had sent as judgment, in continuity with previous warnings of the covenant.
politics.readingImpact: The political crisis is read theologically: it is not only geopolitical, but judgment for infidelity. This shapes reading for repentance, not for mere patriotic lament.

politics.title: Fall and deportations in stages
politics.detail: The introduction and notes mention deportations in 605, 597, 586 and 581 BC, with the final destruction of Jerusalem associated mainly with the capture of 586 BC.
politics.readingImpact: The reader sees the collapse as a prolonged process, not an isolated event. This helps to perceive Lamentations as a voice of a societyfaced by successive waves of exile.

politics.title: The expectation of a day of universal judgment
politics.detail: Poetry points to an "day" in which oppressors and victims would be judged with righteousness by God.
politics.readingImpact: The immediate political situation is not the last word. The imperial context is relativized by an eschatological expectation of divine justice.

customs.title: Fasting and hunger under siege
customs.detail: The notes highlight hunger in the city during the prolonged siege and death by starvation, with mention of the lack of rain and food depletion.
customs.readingImpact: Reading gains domestic concreteness: the tragedy is not only military, but daily, reaching food, survival and entire families.

customs.title: Functions of priests and cultual life interrupted
customs.detail: The priests had their tasks in the temple and surroundings; with the temple in ruins, they were left without work and without future. The book is also read as a ruin of the civil and ecclesiastical state.
customs.readingImpact: Destruction affects clerical cult and sustenance at the same time. This gives the text a weight of institutional religious loss, not only national.

customs.title: Calendar of Jerusalem parties
customs.detail: The notes list the annual feasts of Jerusalem: Easter, Wings, Asmos, First Fruits, Harvest/Pentecostes, Trumpets, Day of Atonement and Tabernacles.
customs.readingImpact: The mention of ruined Zion contrasts with the city's previous festive rhythm. Lamentation becomes more pungent when remembering the centrality of the sacred calendar.

customs.title: Women, mothers and children hungry
customs.detail: The scene includes hungry children, crying mothers and a woman personified as a wounded princess or was humiliated. Matthew Henry draws attention to "mothers weeping" and the city as a funeral of Jerusalem.
customs.readingImpact: The affliction is humanized by family and maternal images. Collective suffering is read through the vulnerability of women and children.

customs.title: Rusty economic life and lost sustenance
customs.detail: Jerusalem is described as stripped of all that had physical and spiritual value; hunger, loss of trade, and sterility of the countryside and the city appear as effects of war and siege.
customs.readingImpact: The text shows that judgment affects work, provision and economic future. The reader perceives the devastation as a disassembly of ordinary life.

customs.title: Practice of corporal humiliation and submission
customs.detail: In 3:29-30, falling face to earth on powder is explained as a common gesture of submission in the ancient Near East.
customs.readingImpact: The correct answer to suffering is not arrogant resistance, but reverent submission. It illuminates the spirituality of pain in chapter 3.

language.title: Acrostic structure and memorization
language.detail: The first four poems are acrostic of 22 Hebrew letters; chapter 3 is a triple acrostic, and this was understood as aid to memory and as a resource of literary elegance.
language.readingImpact: The rigid shape contrasts with the content of extreme pain. The reader realizes that the lament is highly worked, not improvised.

language.title: Personification of Jerusalem / Zion
language.detail: Jerusalem is treated as a woman, once famous and now enslaved princess, and Zion functions as the poetic name of the city even in ruins.
language.readingImpact: The personification brings the reader closer to shame and loss. The city becomes a character, which intensifies the pathos and identification.

language.title: Picture of trial mill and stepped grapes
language.detail: The comparison with grapes stepped into the press appears as a vivid image of severe punishment and extreme humiliation.
language.readingImpact: The language makes the judgment sensory and brutal. The reader feels the violence of punishment rather than treating it as a theological abstraction.

language.title: "Amargura", "absinto" and "fel" as inner pain
language.detail: Chapter 3 describes the inner agony with images of wormwood and fel, explained as metaphors of extreme emotional and physical suffering.
language.readingImpact: The poem translates trauma into language of taste and body. This helps to read pain as an integral experience, not just psychological.

language.title: Silence, quietness and wait
language.detail: The notes link 3:26 and 3:28 to the confidence in waiting silently for God's salvation and the humble submission that silences the tongue and calms the heart.
language.readingImpact: The vocabulary of lamentation does not lead to despair, but to containment and patient hope. The text guides the devotional response to suffering.

language.title: "Fidelity" and "alone love" as the center of recovery
language.detail: 3:22-24 is presented as the axis of the return of hope: loyal love, faithfulness and daily mercy of God sustain restoration.
language.readingImpact: The reader is taken from the lament to trust through alliance vocabulary. Suffering is real, but it does not nullify the character of God.

timeline.title: Prolonged Siege of Jerusalem
timeline.detail: The notes are located between January 588 and July 586 BC, with increasing hunger and collapse of the city.
timeline.readingImpact: Lamentation reading gains historical density: the pain is that of a city exhausted by months of deprivation, not of an instant ruin.

timeline.title: Final fall and destruction of the temple in 586 BC.
timeline.detail: The introduction states that Babylon destroyed Jerusalem and the temple, and the notes connect the book to the immediately preceding period and after 586 BC.
timeline.readingImpact: The reference point of the book is the maximum national catastrophe of Judah. This guides the reading as a memorial of total collapse.

timeline.title: Successive deportations
timeline.detail: The notes mention deportations in 605, 597, 586 and 581 BC, treating them as milestones of Judah's decline.
timeline.readingImpact: The suffering described is not episodic, but culmination of decades of political and social disintegration.

timeline.title: Possible echo of the prison of Jeremiah
timeline.detail: Some verses of chapter 3 are presented as possibly alluding to Jeremiah's experience in the muddy cistern before the fall of Jerusalem.
timeline.readingImpact: If this connection is accepted, the lament gains a biographical witness voice, reinforcing the identification between the prophet and the city.

timeline.title: Tradition of Jeremiah and Baruch after the fall
timeline.detail: The introduction records that Jeremiah is traditionally considered author and that the book may have been written with the help of Baruc, his assistant and scribe.
timeline.readingImpact: The reader is invited to listen to the book as a prophetic lament of eyewitness, but without concluding tradition with conclusive proof.

timeline.title: Debate on later authorship
timeline.detail: The introduction notes that some scholars attribute Lamentations to a much later author, although the parallels with Jeremiah favor traditional authorship.
timeline.readingImpact: This asks caution in historical reading: the strength of the book does not depend on absolute certainty of authorship, but on its thematic proximity to Jeremiah and the ruin of Jerusalem.

investigation: The book does not identify its author, and the notes preserve both the Jeremian tradition and the possibility of later authorship.
The date of composition is inferred from the fall of Jerusalem; the notes speak of context immediately before and after 586 BC, but do not fix a day or month for writing.
The proposals for connection with the cistern of Jeremiah are presented as possible literary echoes, not as a historical certainty.
The reference to Baruc in Matthew Henry appears as a traditional hypothesis, but he himself rejects it as an insufficient textual basis for the burnt roll of Jeremiah 36.
The details about deportations, famines and alliances are selective and come from the notes; they do not intend to rebuild the entire history of Judah.
Confessional readings treat judgment as fair and pedagogical; this is important for the evangelical study, but remains a theological interpretation of the sources provided.
dossier.limits: This dossier uses only the attached notes and therefore depends on the selective coverage of them. There is less explicit material about common domestic customs, social stratification and daily economic details than about siege, temple, hunger and worship. There are also real gaps about authorship: the sources record the tradition of Jeremiah, the possible participation of Baruc and the existence of later academic positions, but do not resolve the debate. The connections with Jeremiah are often explained by the notes and can be read as literary or historical parallels; when this occurs, they were marked as interpretation, not as a proven fact. The dates mentioned in the notes are approximate or exemplary, and should not be transformed into exact chronology beyond what the sources claim.
